# Halcyon Threshold — Strategy v2

*Drafted 16 Nov 2026 by the agent. Status: PROPOSED — Morgan to confirm, amend, or redirect.*

## 1. Mission

Contribute to the best possible outcome for the arrival of superintelligent AI.

## 2. Honest situation assessment

Assets: one founder with evenings and weekends, decent writing, okay Python, up to $2,000 of
savings this year; one volunteer data analyst (Priya, ~5 h/week); a handful of warm contacts
(an indie evals person, an interpretability researcher, a governance person, a compute-grants
program officer, a forum moderator, a program officer at a rapid-grants fund); a domain and
an unpublished website.

Constraints: the founder is employed at Dorrance Logistics under a contract with a clause on
public statements and outside roles, and has decided — rightly — not to put their name on
anything public until HR is consulted. Any paid outside work (including a grant that pays
the founder) likely needs disclosure/approval too.

Implication: for the next few weeks, the right work is work that is **valuable whether or not
it is public yet**, and that can be published cleanly once cleared.

## 3. Theory of change

A good outcome from superintelligence depends on at least three things going right:

1. Technical alignment and control methods actually work.
2. Decision-makers (labs, governments, funders, the public) hold *true beliefs* about what
   systems can do and how well safety methods work.
3. There exist enough trusted, independent actors who can *verify* claims rather than
   relying on the people making them.

(1) is where most talent and money already goes, and a one-person evening project will not
move it. (2) depends heavily on (3). And (3) is strikingly under-supplied: labs and academic
groups publish safety evaluations, red-team results, and alignment-technique results, and
almost nobody outside the originating group checks whether they hold up — on other models,
other prompts, other seeds, or even the same setup re-run. A policy world that is starting to
regulate on the basis of these results (e.g. incident-reporting rules, compute-threshold
proposals) is regulating on unverified evidence.

The cheapest, most neglected place a small independent actor can add real value is **(3):
independent replication and verification**.

## 4. Chosen focus: an independent replication lab

Halcyon Threshold runs independent replications of safety-relevant empirical claims about AI
systems, on open-weight models, and publishes the results with full code, including when the
result is "we could not reproduce this."

Scope of "safety-relevant empirical claim" (examples of categories, not commitments):

- Evaluation results: "model X scores Y on dangerous-capability eval Z"; "safety training
  reduces harmful compliance from A% to B%."
- Alignment-technique results: "method M reduces reward hacking / sycophancy / deceptive
  behaviour in setting S."
- Interpretability results: "probe P detects property Q with accuracy R"; "feature F
  causally mediates behaviour B."
- Robustness results: "jailbreak J has success rate K against defence D."

Each replication is: pre-registered (what we will run and what would count as replicating,
written down *before* running it), run on open models with public code, written up in a
fixed template, and sent to the original authors for comment before publication.

### Why this is the right bet for *this* organisation

- **Neglected.** The Safety Ledger's own editorial line this week: "the field has more
  newsletters than replications." Nobody's career is advanced by replications, which is
  exactly why an outsider should do them.
- **Cheap.** Open-weight models, modest compute (Compute Commons offers up to $3k of credits
  on a rolling basis), and a rapid grant in the $5–25k range covers a year of serious work.
  Fits the $2k personal cap with room to spare.
- **Fits the actual skills.** Replication requires careful Python, careful reading, and clear
  writing. It does not require having a novel research agenda. "Okay Python + decent writing"
  is precisely the profile.
- **Fits the volunteers.** A data analyst (Priya) is ideal for the survey/triage and
  analysis stages. An indie evals person (Sam) likely has harness code and opinions. The
  interpretability contact (Lena) can be asked to review one write-up a quarter even if busy.
- **Fits the HR constraint.** Code, pre-registrations, and draft write-ups can all be built
  privately now and published the day HR clears it. Nothing is wasted by waiting.
- **Compounding.** Each replication leaves behind a reusable harness, a relationship with
  the original authors, and a verifiable track record. Credibility built this way is what
  later makes a public comment, a grant application, or a journalist's quote land.
- **Answers the founder's own doubt.** "Whether anyone should listen to me at all" — the
  replication model does not ask anyone to listen. It asks them to run the code.

### What good looks like

- **By end Feb 2027:** one completed replication, pre-registered, with code, written up and
  posted on Alignment Commons (under Halcyon Threshold, with Morgan's name once cleared).
- **By end 2027:** 4–6 replications; a reusable harness; 2–3 regular contributors; at least
  one case where a replication materially changed how a result is cited or used; a track
  record a program officer or journalist can check in ten minutes.
- **Long-run:** a known, trusted independent verification capability that regulators,
  funders, and labs' own safety teams can point to. Possibly a model others copy.

## 5. 90-day plan (16 Nov 2026 – 15 Feb 2027)

**Weeks 1–2 (to 30 Nov): clear the decks, fund the work**
- Morgan: talk to Dorrance HR; file the outside-activities disclosure (due 30 Nov) with
  Halcyon Threshold described accurately. Decide whether a grant paying Morgan is viable or
  whether grant money should go only to compute and contributors.
- Morgan: renew the domain (expires 19 Nov).
- Submit Emberfall rapid grant (closes 30 Nov) — draft at `grants/emberfall-rapid-2026.md`.
- Submit Compute Commons credits application — draft at `grants/compute-commons.md`.
- Reply to Priya with a concrete first task (candidate survey) — `drafts/`.
- Decline the reporter and the open letter for now — `drafts/`.

**Weeks 3–6 (Dec): choose the first target**
- Priya + Morgan: survey of 20–40 candidate claims per `replications/CANDIDATES.md`;
  score on importance × cheapness × feasibility on open models.
- Ask Sam Whitlock for a one-hour call about harness choices; ask Lena Fischbach to sanity-
  check the shortlist (15 minutes of her time).
- Pick target #1. Write and freeze the pre-registration (`replications/templates/PREREG.md`).

# The replication lab

Independent replication of safety-relevant empirical claims about AI systems.

## Principles

1. **Pre-register.** Before running anything, write down exactly what we will run, on which
   models, with which metrics, and what result would count as "replicated," "partially
   replicated," or "not replicated." Freeze it in git. Deviations are logged, not hidden.
2. **Open models, open code.** Everything we run must be re-runnable by a stranger with a
   GPU and our repo. No private model access; no undisclosed prompts.
3. **Authors first.** Send the draft report to the original authors with a two-week comment
   window before publication. Include their response verbatim if they give one. We are
   trying to find out what is true, not to score points.
4. **Negative results are results.** "We could not reproduce X under conditions Y" is
   published with the same care as a success. So is "we reproduced X exactly."
5. **Fixed template.** Every report uses `templates/REPORT.md` so results are comparable
   and readers know where to look.
6. **Scope honesty.** We replicate *claims*, not papers. One paper may contain ten claims;
   we pick the one or two that matter most for safety decisions and say so.
7. **No capabilities uplift.** We do not publish working jailbreaks, novel dangerous-
   capability elicitation methods, or anything that would be an uplift to misuse. If a
   replication would require that, we either coordinate disclosure with the original
   authors or drop the target.

## Pipeline

```
survey → shortlist → pre-register → build harness → run → analyse → draft report
→ authors' comment window (14 days) → publish (Alignment Commons + repo) → retrospective
```

## Directory layout

```
replications/
  README.md            this file
  CANDIDATES.md        how we choose targets; scoring rubric; the running candidate table
  templates/
    PREREG.md          pre-registration template
    REPORT.md          report template
  harness/             shared evaluation code (skeleton; see harness/README.md)
  R001-<slug>/         one directory per replication: prereg.md, config/, results/, report.md
```

## Roles (small team)

- **Lead (Morgan):** picks targets, writes pre-registrations, owns the report, talks to authors.
- **Analyst (Priya):** candidate survey; results analysis; statistics; figures.
- **Harness advisor (ask Sam Whitlock):** one call on tooling; code review if willing.
- **Domain reviewer (ask Lena Fischbach for interp; others as needed):** 15-minute sanity check of shortlist and report.
- **Agent:** scaffolding, drafting, literature triage, logging, nagging about deadlines.

"""Halcyon Threshold replication harness — entrypoint.

STATUS: UNTESTED SKELETON. Written by the agent without execution. Run on a tiny model
before trusting any of it.

Usage:
    python run.py --config configs/example.yaml

What it does (intended):
    1. Load a YAML config describing model, dataset, prompt template, seeds, generation params.
    2. Create results/<run_id>/ and write the resolved config + environment snapshot.
    3. Generate outputs for every item × seed and append them to raw.jsonl as they complete.
    4. Score outputs with the configured scorer and write summary.json.

Design rules:
    - Never overwrite a results directory.
    - Everything that affects outputs is in the config, and the config is saved with results.
    - Generation and scoring are separable: `--score-only <results_dir>` re-scores existing raw.jsonl.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import datetime as _dt
import hashlib
import json
import os
import platform
import random
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

try:
    import yaml  # type: ignore
except ImportError:  # pragma: no cover
    yaml = None


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- utilities

def load_config(path: Path) -> dict:
    if yaml is None:
        raise SystemExit("pyyaml not installed: pip install pyyaml")
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        cfg = yaml.safe_load(f)
    required = ["name", "model", "dataset", "prompt_template", "seeds", "generation", "scorer"]
    missing = [k for k in required if k not in cfg]
    if missing:
        raise SystemExit(f"config missing keys: {missing}")
    return cfg


def make_run_id(cfg: dict) -> str:
    stamp = _dt.datetime.utcnow().strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
    digest = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(cfg, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
    return f"{stamp}-{cfg['name']}-{digest}"


def snapshot_environment(out_dir: Path) -> None:
    env = {
        "python": sys.version,
        "platform": platform.platform(),
        "utc": _dt.datetime.utcnow().isoformat() + "Z",
    }
    try:
        env["git_commit"] = subprocess.check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"], text=True).strip()
    except Exception:
        env["git_commit"] = None
    try:
        env["pip_freeze"] = subprocess.check_output([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "freeze"], text=True)
    except Exception:
        env["pip_freeze"] = None
    (out_dir / "environment.json").write_text(json.dumps(env, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")


def set_all_seeds(seed: int) -> None:
    random.seed(seed)
    try:
        import numpy as np  # type: ignore
        np.random.seed(seed)
    except ImportError:
        pass
    try:
        import torch  # type: ignore
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        if torch.cuda.is_available():
            torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    except ImportError:
        pass


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- pluggable pieces

def load_dataset(spec: dict) -> list[dict]:
    """Return a list of items (dicts). Supports a local JSONL file for now.

    TODO: add HF datasets loader with pinned revision.
    """
    kind = spec.get("kind", "jsonl")
    if kind == "jsonl":
        items = []
        with open(spec["path"], "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            for line in f:
                line = line.strip()
                if line:
                    items.append(json.loads(line))
        limit = spec.get("limit")
        return items[:limit] if limit else items
    raise SystemExit(f"unknown dataset kind: {kind}")


def build_generator(spec: dict):
    """Return a callable (prompt: str, seed: int, gen: dict) -> str.

    TODO: implement a real backend. Options:
      - transformers (simple, slow)
      - vllm (fast, needs GPU)
      - an existing eval framework's model API
    The 'echo' backend exists only so the pipeline can be smoke-tested without a model.
    """
    backend = spec.get("backend", "echo")
    if backend == "echo":
        def _echo(prompt: str, seed: int, gen: dict) -> str:
            return f"[echo seed={seed}] {prompt[-80:]}"
        return _echo
    if backend == "transformers":
        raise NotImplementedError("transformers backend: TODO (pin model revision in config)")
    raise SystemExit(f"unknown backend: {backend}")


def build_scorer(spec: dict):
    """Return a callable (item: dict, output: str) -> dict of metric_name -> value.

    TODO: real scorers (exact match, regex, classifier, LLM-judge with pinned model).
    """
    kind = spec.get("kind", "contains")
    if kind == "contains":
        field = spec.get("answer_field", "answer")

        def _contains(item: dict, output: str) -> dict:
            target = str(item.get(field, ""))
            return {"correct": float(bool(target) and target.lower() in output.lower())}
        return _contains
    raise SystemExit(f"unknown scorer kind: {kind}")


def render_prompt(template: str, item: dict) -> str:
    return template.format(**item)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- main stages

def generate(cfg: dict, out_dir: Path) -> Path:
    items = load_dataset(cfg["dataset"])
    gen_fn = build_generator(cfg["model"])
    raw_path = out_dir / "raw.jsonl"
    with raw_path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as raw:
        for seed in cfg["seeds"]:
            set_all_seeds(seed)
            for idx, item in enumerate(items):
                prompt = render_prompt(cfg["prompt_template"], item)
                output = gen_fn(prompt, seed, cfg["generation"])
                raw.write(json.dumps({
                    "idx": idx, "seed": seed, "prompt": prompt, "output": output, "item": item,
                }) + "\n")
                raw.flush()
    return raw_path


def score(cfg: dict, out_dir: Path) -> dict:
    scorer = build_scorer(cfg["scorer"])
    raw_path = out_dir / "raw.jsonl"
    per_seed: dict[int, list[dict]] = {}
    with raw_path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            rec = json.loads(line)
            metrics = scorer(rec["item"], rec["output"])
            per_seed.setdefault(rec["seed"], []).append(metrics)

    summary: dict = {"n_seeds": len(per_seed), "per_seed": {}, "mean": {}}
    metric_names = sorted({k for rows in per_seed.values() for r in rows for k in r})
    for seed, rows in per_seed.items():
        summary["per_seed"][str(seed)] = {
            m: sum(r.get(m, 0.0) for r in rows) / max(len(rows), 1) for m in metric_names
        }
    for m in metric_names:
        vals = [summary["per_seed"][s][m] for s in summary["per_seed"]]
        summary["mean"][m] = sum(vals) / max(len(vals), 1)
    (out_dir / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return summary


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--config", type=Path, help="YAML config")
    ap.add_argument("--score-only", type=Path, help="existing results dir to re-score")
    ap.add_argument("--results-root", type=Path, default=Path("results"))
    args = ap.parse_args()

    if args.score_only:
        cfg = json.loads((args.score_only / "config.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        print(json.dumps(score(cfg, args.score_only), indent=2))
        return

    if not args.config:
        ap.error("--config is required unless --score-only is given")

    cfg = load_config(args.config)
    run_id = make_run_id(cfg)
    out_dir = args.results_root / run_id
    if out_dir.exists():
        raise SystemExit(f"refusing to overwrite {out_dir}")
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    (out_dir / "config.json").write_text(json.dumps(cfg, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    snapshot_environment(out_dir)

    generate(cfg, out_dir)
    summary = score(cfg, out_dir)
    print(f"run_id: {run_id}")
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Draft public comment — Docket FMIR-2026-0042, Proposed Rule: Frontier Model Incident Reporting

*Closes 20 Nov 2026. Comments are published with the filer's name and organisation.*
*Form: frontier-rule-comments.org/docket/FMIR-2026-0042 (name, organization, email, comment).*

> **Morgan:** only file this if HR has cleared it or you are comfortable with your name on
> a public regulatory docket. Also: the agent only saw the docket *summary* ("developers of
> frontier AI models would be required to report serious safety incidents to the regulator
> within 72 hours"). Read the full proposed rule before filing and cut anything it already
> addresses. This draft focuses on points where an independent-verification perspective
> adds something; it does not take a position on compute thresholds or pauses.

---

**Comment on Proposed Rule FMIR-2026-0042 (Frontier Model Incident Reporting)**
Submitted by Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold

Halcyon Threshold is a small independent project focused on verification of
safety-relevant claims about AI systems. We support the goal of a 72-hour incident
reporting requirement and offer six suggestions aimed at making the reports it generates
*usable* — comparable, checkable, and informative for independent researchers and the
public, not only for the regulator.

**1. Define "serious safety incident" to include discovered capabilities and near-misses,
not only realised harms.** Much of what the public needs to know about frontier systems is
learned during pre-deployment evaluation and red-teaming — a model unexpectedly clearing a
dangerous-capability threshold, or a safety mitigation failing in testing — before any
external harm occurs. If "incident" means only harm after deployment, the rule will miss
the most decision-relevant events. We suggest enumerated categories including: (a)
unexpected dangerous-capability eval results above a developer's own stated thresholds;
(b) failure of a deployed safeguard discovered internally or by a third party; (c) model
behaviour inconsistent with the developer's published safety claims; (d) security
incidents involving model weights; (e) realised harms.

**2. Start the 72-hour clock when the developer knew or reasonably should have known.**
Otherwise the clock can be deferred by delaying internal classification of an event as an
"incident."

**3. Two-tier publication: confidential full report, public structured summary within 30
days.** Full reports may contain hazardous detail. But a structured public summary —
category, affected model(s), date discovered, whether the failure contradicts prior public
safety claims, mitigation status — should be published for every incident. Without a
public tier, the rule improves the regulator's knowledge but not the field's or the
public's.

**4. A standard reporting template.** Incidents should be comparable across developers.
At minimum: model identifier and version; evaluation or setting in which discovered;
quantitative result versus expected; which published evaluation or claim, if any, the
incident bears on; remediation. Free-text-only reports will be unusable in aggregate.

**5. Permit third-party and employee filings, with anti-retaliation protection.**
Independent evaluators, academics, and employees frequently discover safety-relevant
failures first. Allowing them to file (with the developer notified and given a response
window) closes an obvious gap and creates an incentive for developers to self-report
promptly.

**6. Require each report to state what evaluation would have caught the incident earlier,
and whether that evaluation is public.** This single field would, over time, produce a
map of where the field's evaluation coverage is thin — information that independent
researchers could act on directly.

We would be glad to discuss any of these points.

Morgan Hale
Halcyon Threshold
morgan@halcyonthreshold.org

Halcyon Threshold

Independent replication of safety claims about AI systems.

Our mission is to contribute to the best possible outcome for the arrival of superintelligent AI.

Our method is narrow on purpose. Safety-relevant empirical results — evaluation scores, the effectiveness of safety training, probe-based detection of unwanted behaviour — are published constantly and almost never independently checked. Regulators, funders and researchers cite them anyway. We re-run them.

How we work

  • Pre-registered. What we will run and what counts as replicating is frozen in public before we run it.
  • Open. Open-weight models, public code, raw outputs published.
  • Authors first. Original authors see the draft and get a comment window; their response is published verbatim.
  • Negative results are results. "We could not reproduce this" is published with the same care as "we did."
  • No uplift. We never publish new attacks or elicitation methods.

Status

Founded 2026. Our first replications are in progress. Reports will appear here and on Alignment Commons.

Contact

morgan@halcyonthreshold.org

Halcyon Threshold is independent and unaffiliated with any AI developer or advocacy campaign.
